---
title: "Liver - Gray's Anatomy"
---

## Introduction to the Liver

- The liver is the largest abdominal organ.
- Occupies a substantial portion of the upper abdominal cavity.
- Occupies most of the right hypochondriac and epigastric regions.
- Frequently extends into the left hypochondriac region as far as the left anterior axillary line.
- As the body grows from infancy to adulthood, the liver rapidly increases in size.

## Growth and Weight

- Period of growth reaches a plateau around 18 years.
- Followed by a gradual decrease in liver weight during middle age.
- Liver-to-body weight ratio decreases with growth from infancy to adulthood.
- Liver weight is 4–5% of body weight in infancy.
- Decreases to approximately 2% in adulthood.

## Size and Shape Variations

- Size differs between sexes (smaller in females).
- Size varies with body size (enlarges with fat deposition in obese individuals).
- Overall wedge shape, partly determined by the form of the upper abdominal cavity.
- Narrow end of the wedge lies towards the left hypochondriac region.
- Anterior edge points anteriorly and inferiorly.

## Contours and Capsule

- Superior and right lateral aspects are shaped by the anterolateral abdominal and thoracic walls, and the diaphragm.
- Inferior aspect is shaped by adjacent viscera.
- Fibrous capsule is no longer considered important in maintaining liver shape.
- Capsule allows expansion when liver hypertrophies (due to disease, resection, or embolisation).

## Color and Texture

- The liver is reddish-brown.
- Assumes a more yellowish tinge and rounding of edges with increasing fat (steatosis).
- Common in obese individuals or those who drink excessive alcohol.
- Gains a bluish tinge with venous outflow obstruction (Budd–Chiari syndrome).
- Also bluish in congestive heart failure and administration of some chemotherapy.
- Texture is usually soft to firm, depending on blood volume, adipose, and fibrous tissue content.

## Metabolic Functions

- Removal and breakdown of toxic materials from blood.
- Regulation of blood glucose and lipids.
- Storage of vitamins, iron, and micronutrients.
- Synthesis of proteins and clotting factors.
- Metabolism of amino acids.
- Bile production.

## Thermal and Immune Functions

- Involved in a plethora of biochemical reactions.
- Most processes are exothermic, providing substantial thermal energy, especially at rest.
- Populated by phagocytic macrophages (mononuclear phagocyte system).
- Removes particulates from bloodstream.
- Important site of haemopoiesis in the fetus.
- Site of extramedullary haemopoiesis in haematological disease.

## Surfaces of the Liver

- Usually described as having superior, anterior, right, posterior, and inferior surfaces.
- Distinct inferior border present.
- However, superior, anterior, and right surfaces are continuous without definable borders.
- Grouping them as the **diaphragmatic surface** is more appropriate.
- Mostly separated from the inferior, or **visceral surface**, by a narrow inferior border.

## Inferior Border

- At the infrasternal angle, adjacent to anterolateral abdominal wall.
- Accessible to physical examination by percussion.
- Not usually palpable except on deep inspiration.
- In the midline, near the transpyloric plane.
- In females and children, often projects inferior to the right costal arch.

## Superior Surface

- Largest surface.
- Lies immediately below the diaphragm.
- Separated by peritoneum, except for a small triangular area where falciform ligament layers diverge.
- Mostly inferior to right superior aspect of diaphragm.
- Shallow cardiac impression centrally (corresponds to heart above central tendon).
- Left side lies inferior to part of left side of diaphragm.

## Anterior Surface

- Approximately triangular and convex.
- Covered by peritoneum, except at attachment of falciform ligament.
- Much of it in contact with anterior attachment of diaphragm.
- On the right: separated from pleura and 6th to 10th ribs and costal cartilages.
- On the left: separated from 7th and 8th costal cartilages.

## Right Surface

- Covered by peritoneum.
- Lies adjacent to right superior aspect of diaphragm.
- Separates it from right lung, parietal pleura, and 7th to 11th ribs.
- Right lung and basal pleura lie superior and lateral to proximal third.
- Diaphragm, costodiaphragmatic recess, and 9th/10th ribs lie lateral to middle/inferior thirds.
- Rarely, right colic flexure lies here (Chilaiditi syndrome).

## Posterior Surface

- Convex, wide on right, narrow on left.
- Median concavity corresponds to forward convexity of vertebral column.
- Attached to diaphragm by loose connective tissue, forming 'bare area'.
- Inferior vena cava lies in a groove or tunnel in medial end of bare area.
- Left of IVC groove: formed by caudate lobe.

## Posterior Surface Relations

- Caudate lobe covered by peritoneum continuous with coronary ligament and lesser omentum.
- Retrocaval (hepatocaval) ligament connects caudate lobe and right liver posterior to IVC.
- Almost always includes a small hepatic vein draining into posterior IVC.
- Caudate lobe related to diaphragmatic crura and right inferior phrenic artery.
- Separated from descending thoracic aorta by these structures.

## Posterior Surface Fissures

- Fissure for ligamentum venosum separates caudate lobe from left lobe.
- Cuts deeply in front of caudate lobe.
- Contains two layers of lesser omentum.
- Posterior surface of left lobe bears shallow oesophageal impression near superior end of fissure.
- Left of oesophageal impression: related to fundus of stomach.
- Together, these relations make up the 'bed' of the liver.

## Inferior Surface

- Bounded by inferior edge of liver.
- Blends with posterior surface at lesser omentum, porta hepatis, and inferior layer of coronary ligament.
- Marked near midline by sharp fissure containing round ligament (ligamentum teres hepatis).
- Gallbladder usually lies in shallow fossa (can have mesentery or be intrahepatic).
- Quadrate lobe lies between fissure for round ligament and gallbladder.

## Inferior Surface Relations

- Left lobe: related to fundus of stomach and superior aspect of lesser omentum.
- Quadrate lobe: adjacent to pylorus, superior part of duodenum, inferior part of lesser omentum.
- Occasionally, transverse colon lies between duodenum and quadrate lobe.
- Right of gallbladder: related to right colic flexure, right suprarenal gland, right kidney, superior part of duodenum.

## Supports of the Liver

- Stabilised by static and dynamic factors.
- **Primary factors:** Suspensory attachments of IVC, hepatic veins, coronary and triangular ligaments.
- **Secondary factors:** Support from right kidney, right colic flexure, duodenopancreatic complex.
- **Tertiary factors:** Attachment of falciform ligament to anterolateral abdominal wall and diaphragm.

## Surgical Implications of Liver Supports

- Important for understanding pathophysiology of blunt liver trauma.
- Important for stability of transplanted liver grafts.
- IVC and hepatic veins (especially right) are most important anatomical supports.
- Other factors: positive intra-abdominal pressure and diaphragm movement during respiration.

## Gross Anatomical Lobes

- Historically divided based on external appearance.
- Four lobes: right, left, caudate, and quadrate.
- Defined partly by peritoneal ligamentous attachments.
- Additional liver lobes reported but rare.

## Right Lobe

- Largest in volume.
- Contributes to all surfaces of the liver.
- Divided from left lobe by falciform ligament anteriorly/superiorly.
- Divided inferiorly by ligamentum venosum and fissure for round ligament.
- Porta hepatis separates caudate lobe (posterior) and quadrate lobe (anterior).
- Gallbladder lies in shallow fossa between quadrate and right lobe.

## Left Lobe

- Smaller of the two main lobes.
- Nearly as large as right lobe in young children.
- Lies to the left of falciform ligament with no subdivisions.
- Substantially thinner than right lobe.
- Thin apex points into left upper quadrant.

## Quadrate Lobe

- Prominence on inferior surface to right of round ligament groove.
- Anatomically part of right lobe.
- Vascular inflow from left branch of hepatic portal vein and left hepatic artery.
- Biliary outflow to left hepatic duct.
- Bounded by gallbladder fossa (right), inferior border (anterior), round ligament fissure (left), porta hepatis (posterior).
- Morphology varies among individuals.

## Caudate Lobe

- Prominence on inferior and posterior surfaces to right of ligamentum venosum groove.
- Lies posterior to porta hepatis and hepatogastric ligament.
- Groove for IVC lies to its right.
- Right margin (paracaval portion) challenging to define precisely.
- Continues into superior surface on right of superior end of fissure for ligamentum venosum.
- Grossly arises from right lobe but functionally separate.

## Functional Anatomical Divisions

- Based on Couinaud's division into eight functional segments.
- Based on distribution of portal venous branches in parenchyma.
- Intrahepatic biliary anatomy enhanced by Hjortsjö (1951) and Healey & Schroy (1953).
- 'French' model: portal and hepatic veins.
- 'American' model: bile ducts.
- Brisbane nomenclature (2000) introduced to improve terminologies (sections vs. sectors).

![Figure 69.4: The fissures and sectors of the liver. (Right lateral = right posterior; right medial = right anterior.)](figure_69_4.png)

## Portal Sectors

- Liver divided into four portal sectors:
  - Right anterior
  - Right posterior
  - Left medial
  - Left lateral
- Divided by four main branches of hepatic portal vein.
- Three main hepatic veins lie between sectors as intersectoral veins.
- Intersectoral planes = portal fissures (or scissures).
- Each sector subdivided into segments (usually two) based on tertiary divisions of Glissonian sheaths.

## Fissures of the Liver

- Knowledge essential for liver surgery.
- **Major portal fissures:** Main, left, right. Not visible on surface. Contain main hepatic veins.
- **Minor fissures:** Umbilical, venous, fissure of Gans. Visible as physical clefts.
- **Accessory fissures:** Rare.
- Diaphragmatic sulci seen in 40% of livers (usually superior surface of right lobe).

## Main Portal Fissure

- Also called Cantlie's line.
- Extends from midpoint of gallbladder fossa to midpoint of IVC.
- Contains middle hepatic vein.
- Separates liver into right and left hemilivers.
- Segments V and VIII lie immediately to right.
- Segment IV lies immediately to left.

## Left Portal Fissure

- Divides left hemiliver into left medial and lateral sectors.
- Extends from midpoint of inferior edge (between falciform and left triangular ligaments) to confluence of left and middle hepatic veins.
- Contains left hepatic vein.
- Separates left medial (anterior) and left lateral (posterior) sectors.
- Segment III lies anteriorly, Segment II posteriorly.

## Right Portal Fissure

- Divides right hemiliver into right posterior and anterior sectors.
- Plane is the most variable of portal fissures.
- Runs diagonally through anatomical right lobe.
- Divides right anterior sector (V, VIII) from right posterior sector (VI, VII).
- Contains right hepatic vein.
- Traverses thickest portion of liver commonly transected during resection.

## Umbilical Fissure

- Fissure for round ligament of liver.
- Separates segments II and III from segment IV.
- Contains major tributary of left hepatic vein (umbilical fissure vein).
- Marked anteriorly by falciform ligament, inferiorly by round ligament.
- May be covered by avascular bridge of liver tissue between segments III and IV.
- Contains umbilical portion of left branch of hepatic portal vein.

## Umbilical Fissure Surgical Importance

- Contains segmental bile ducts converging to form left hepatic duct.
- Contains terminal branches of left hepatic artery.
- Offers direct surgical access to left branch of hepatic portal vein.
- Essential knowledge for:
  - Cholangiocarcinoma surgery
  - Restoring intrahepatic portal blood flow
  - Split liver transplantation
  - Live donor liver transplantation

## Venous Fissure

- Fissure for ligamentum venosum.
- Directly continuous with umbilical fissure on undersurface.
- Contains ligamentum venosum (obliterated ductus venosus).
- Lies between caudate lobe and segment II.

## Fissure of Gans

- Also called Rouvière's sulcus.
- Lies on undersurface of right lobe.
- Posterior to gallbladder fossa and anterior to segment I.
- Occurs in over 80% of normal livers.
- Often marks variable site of division of portal pedicle to right posterior sector.
- Useful landmark during laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

## Sectors and Segments

- **Right posterior sector:** Segments VI and VII.
- **Right anterior sector:** Segments V and VIII.
- **Left medial sector:** Segment IV (and part of I).
- **Left lateral sector:** Segments II and III.
- Segments numbered clockwise from below, starting with I ending with VIII.

## Segment I

- Corresponds to anatomical caudate lobe.
- Supplied by branches of left and right hepatic portal veins.
- Arterial branches from left and/or right hepatic arteries.
- Lies posterior to segment IV.
- Caudate process extends to left, posterior to hepatogastric ligament.
- Straddles the inferior vena cava.

## Segment I: Subdivisions and Drainage

- Left half directly adjacent to segment II.
- Right half wrapped around retrohepatic IVC.
- European literature: subdivided into caudate process, caudate lobe (Spiegel's lobe), paracaval portion.
- Asian literature: right and left subdivisions.
- Perivascular fibrous capsules arise from both right and left main capsules.
- Venous drainage directly into IVC by multiple small tributaries (usually inferior third).

## Segment I: Biliary Drainage

- Bile ducts closely related to confluence of right and left hepatic ducts.
- Excision of bile duct tumours at porta hepatis usually requires removal of segment I.
- Caudate bile duct tributaries have serpiginous course anterior to retrohepatic IVC.
- Close to surface adhering to IVC.
- Often leak bile when liver dissected free from IVC.
- May drain into left or right hepatic ducts or both.

## Segment II

- Lies posterolateral to left portal fissure.
- Often has only one perivascular fibrous capsule.
- Drains into left hepatic vein.
- Rarely, a separate vein drains directly into IVC.

## Segment III

- Lies between umbilical fissure and left portal fissure.
- One to three perivascular fibrous capsules supply it.
- Drains into left hepatic vein.
- Very rarely drains to middle hepatic vein.
- If draining to middle hepatic vein, reconstruction is required following right hepatectomy or split liver transplantation.

## Segment IV

- Lies between umbilical fissure and main portal fissure.
- Anterior to segment I.
- Supplied by three to five perivascular fibrous capsules (arising in umbilical fissure).
- Origins often close to capsules supplying segments II and III.
- Typically divided into IVa (superior) and IVb (inferior).
- Subdivision relevant to transverse hepatectomy (removing IVb, V, VI).
- Usually drains into middle hepatic vein, sometimes left.

## Segment V

- Inferior segment of right anterior sector.
- Lies between middle and right hepatic veins.
- Size is variable.
- Number of perivascular fibrous capsules varies.
- Supplied from right anterior capsule.
- Venous drainage usually into right and middle hepatic veins.
- Can drain directly into IVC via inferior right hepatic vein.

## Segment VI

- Forms inferior part of right posterior sector.
- Posterior to right portal fissure.
- Two to three branches from right posterior perivascular fibrous capsule.
- Occasionally arises directly from right pedicle.
- Venous drainage usually into right hepatic vein.
- Can drain directly into IVC via inferior right hepatic vein.

## Segment VII

- Forms superior part of right posterior sector.
- Lies posterior to right hepatic vein.
- Sheath to segment VII is often single.
- Venous drainage into right hepatic vein.
- Occasionally drains directly into IVC.

## Segment VIII

- Superior part of right anterior sector.
- Right anterior sectoral sheath ends in segment VIII.
- Supplies it after giving off branches to segment V.
- Venous drainage to right and middle hepatic veins.

## Peritoneal Attachments and Ligaments

- Liver attached to anterolateral abdominal wall, diaphragm, and viscera by peritoneal ligaments.
- Key ligaments:
  - Falciform ligament
  - Round ligament
  - Coronary ligament
  - Triangular ligaments
  - Lesser omentum
  - Ligamentum venosum

## Falciform Ligament and Round Ligament

- Falciform ligament attaches liver to anterolateral abdominal wall.
- Derived from ventral mesogastrium.
- Two layers pass posteriorly and to the right.
- Right leaf continuous with superior layer of coronary ligament.
- Left layer continuous with anterior layer of left triangular ligament.
- Round ligament is obliterated remnant of fetal left umbilical vein.

## Round Ligament Details

- Runs in inferior free border of falciform ligament.
- Continues into fissure on inferior surface.
- In fetal life, opened into left branch of hepatic portal vein.
- Usually obliterates soon after birth.
- Sometimes remains partially patent for surgical access.
- Reopens in portal hypertension (cirrhosis) as a collateral channel.

## Surgical Importance of Round Ligament

- Divided in upper abdominal surgery for access/mobilisation.
- Vascularised by arterial branches (mainly artery to segment IV).
- Anastomoses with superior epigastric artery.
- Important to ligate/coagulate during division.
- Guide to segment III hepatic duct in hepaticojejunostomy.
- Guide to left branch of hepatic portal vein in mesenterico-portal vein bypass.

## Coronary Ligament

- Formed by reflection of peritoneum from diaphragm to superior/posterior surfaces of right lobe.
- Large triangular 'bare area' lies between two layers.
- Liver attached to diaphragm by loose connective tissue.
- Continuous inferiorly with anterior pararenal space.
- Right layers converge laterally to form right triangular ligament.
- Left layers form left triangular ligament.
- Division allows right lobe rotation to expose lateral IVC.

## Triangular Ligaments

- **Left triangular ligament:** Double layer of peritoneum over superior border of left lobe.
  - Lies in front of abdominal oesophagus and fundus of stomach.
  - Division allows mobilisation of left lobe.
  - Important stabilising factor for left lobe after right lobe excision.
- **Right triangular ligament:** Short structure at right lateral limit of bare area.

## Lesser Omentum

- Double layer of peritoneum from lesser curvature of stomach and proximal duodenum to inferior surface of liver.
- Free margin contains portal triad (hepatic portal vein, bile duct, hepatic artery).
- Attachment to liver is L-shaped.
- Vertical component follows fissure for ligamentum venosum.
- Horizontal component runs in porta hepatis.
- May contain replaced or accessory left hepatic artery.

## Ligamentum Venosum

- Obliterated venous connection in fetus between left branch of hepatic portal vein and left hepatic vein.
- (Remnant of ductus venosus).
- Used as guide to gain control of left hepatic vein outside liver during surgery.
- Dividing it allows access to angle between left and middle hepatic veins.
- Helpful in left liver resection with caudate lobe preservation.

## Porta Hepatis and Hilar Plate

- Porta hepatis: deep transverse fissure on inferior surface.
- Between quadrate lobe (anterior) and caudate process (posterior).
- Contains: hepatic portal vein, hepatic artery, hepatic nervous plexuses.
- Also contains: right/left hepatic ducts, lymphatic vessels.
- Hepatic ducts usually lie anterior to portal vein.
- Hepatic artery lies between the two.

## Perivascular Fibrous Capsule at Porta Hepatis

- All structures enveloped in loose connective tissue (perivascular fibrous capsule).
- Continuous with fibrous capsule of liver.
- Dense aggregation just superior to porta hepatis = 'hilar plate'.
- Division/lowering of hilar plate essential for optimum surgical access to left hepatic duct.

## Hepatoduodenal Ligament and Pringle Manoeuvre

- Structures extend between porta hepatis and superior border of duodenum in free edge of hepatoduodenal ligament.
- Rapid control of vessels (hepatic pedicle) obtained by compressing them in free edge of lesser omentum.
- **Pringle manoeuvre:**
  - Divide lesser omentum to left of structures.
  - Pass tape around them through omental foramen.

## Hepatic Ducts

- **Left hepatic duct:** Extrahepatic, descends obliquely along undersurface of segment IV. Useful for biliary-enteric bypass.
- **Right hepatic duct:** More intrahepatic. Extending anastomosis onto it necessitates incision in gallbladder fossa.

## Perivascular Fibrous Capsules (Glissonian Sheaths)

- Fibrous capsule (Glisson capsule) condenses around branches of portal triad.
- Occurs as they enter liver and subdivide into segmental branches.
- Single fibrous capsule surrounds each bile duct, hepatic artery, and portal vein.
- Portal vein surrounded by loose connective tissue (easy dissection).
- Fibrous tissue around bile ducts and arteries is tougher (difficult dissection).
- Facilitates surgical control of vasculobiliary pedicles.

## Vascular Supply and Lymphatic Drainage

- **Supply:** Hepatic artery, hepatic portal vein.
- **Drainage:** Hepatic veins.
- Portal vein, artery, and common hepatic duct ascend in lesser omentum to porta hepatis.
- Each usually bifurcates.
- Lymphatic vessels descend from porta hepatis alongside portal vein and artery.
- Hepatic veins leave posterior surface directly into IVC.

## Hepatic Artery: Origin and Course

- During fetal/early postnatal life: largest branch of coeliac trunk.
- In adults: intermediate in size between left gastric and splenic arteries.
- Gives off right gastric and gastroduodenal arteries.
- Subdivided into:
  - **Common hepatic artery:** Coeliac trunk to origin of gastroduodenal artery.
  - **Proper hepatic artery:** From gastroduodenal origin to bifurcation.

## Hepatic Artery: Relations and Branches

- Ascends anterior to hepatic portal vein and medial to bile duct.
- Within free margin of hepatoduodenal ligament (anterior wall of omental foramen).
- Left and right hepatic arteries arise at variable level below porta hepatis.
- Right hepatic artery typically crosses posterior (occasionally anterior) to common hepatic duct.
- Cystic artery usually arises from right hepatic artery lateral to portal vein.

## Right Hepatic Artery

- Proximity to bile duct bifurcation means it is often involved/encased by hilar cholangiocarcinoma.
- More frequently involved than left hepatic artery.
- Occasionally crosses anterior to common hepatic duct (vulnerable to injury in biliary surgery).
- Almost always divides into:
  - **Anterior branch:** supplies segments V and VIII. Often supplies segment I and gallbladder.
  - **Posterior branch:** supplies segments VI and VII.
- Segmental arteries are macroscopically end arteries.

![Figure 69.9: The hepatic artery. A, Branches. B, Usual relations of hepatic artery, bile duct and portal vein. C, CT mesenteric angiogram. D, Digital subtraction angiogram.](figure_69_9.png)

## Anatomical Variants of Hepatic Artery

- Found in about one-third of individuals.
- Important for surgical and interventional radiological procedures.
- **Accessory artery:** Supplies part of liver in addition to normal artery.
- **Replaced hepatic artery:** Does not originate from orthodox position, provides sole supply.
- Most variants are replaced arteries (require reconstruction if divided during transplantation).

## Types of Replaced Arteries

- **Replaced common hepatic artery:** Can arise from superior mesenteric artery (SMA). Suspected by relatively superficial portal vein.
- **Replaced or accessory right hepatic artery:** Arises from SMA. Runs posterior to portal vein and bile duct. Palpable pulsation posterior to portal vein.
- **Replaced or accessory left hepatic artery:** Arises from left gastric artery. Enters liver through umbilical fissure. Can be injured during stomach mobilisation.

## Clinical Importance of Arterial Variants

- Replaced arteries can be life-saving in bile duct cancer.
- Further away from bile duct, spared from infiltration, making tumour excision feasible.
- Knowledge essential for whole and split liver transplantation.
- Presence often requires reconstruction.
- **Segment IV artery variation:** Most commonly arises from left hepatic artery, but in up to 30% arises from right or proper hepatic artery. Important during right liver donation.

## Veins of the Liver

- Two venous systems:
  1. **Portal venous system:** Conveys blood from GI tract to liver.
  2. **Hepatic venous system:** Drains blood from liver parenchyma into IVC.

## Hepatic Portal Vein: Formation

- Formed posterior to neck of pancreas.
- Usually from convergence of superior mesenteric and splenic veins.
- Origin in transpyloric plane (between L1 and L2 vertebrae).
- Approximately 8 cm long.
- Ascends obliquely to right, posterior to superior duodenum, bile duct, gastroduodenal artery.
- Anterior to IVC.

## Hepatic Portal Vein: Course and Relations

- Enters hepatoduodenal ligament.
- Ascends anterior to omental foramen.
- Reaches right end of porta hepatis, divides into right and left main branches.
- Lies posterior to both bile duct and hepatic artery.
- Surrounded by hepatic nervous plexus, lymphatics, lymph nodes.
- Contains smooth muscle in wall. Valveless.

## Figure 69.12: Coronal CT of Portal Veins

![Figure 69.12: Coronal CT of abdomen and pelvis showing superior mesenteric and hepatic portal veins.](figure_69_12.png)

## Portal Vein Tributaries and Branches

- **Extrahepatic tributaries:** Left gastric vein, posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal vein.
- **Left branch:** Longer extrahepatic course (4-5 cm), more horizontal, smaller calibre. Gives branches to segment I, IV. Continues in umbilical fissure giving branches to III, IV. Receives obliterated left umbilical vein.
- **Right branch:** 2-3 cm long. Divides into right medial (anterior) sectoral (V, VIII) and right lateral (posterior) sectoral (VI, VII). Can give branch to segment I.

## Figure 69.13: Intrahepatic Portal Branches

![Figure 69.13: The hepatic portal vein and its intrahepatic branches.](figure_69_13.png)

## Hepatic Portal Vein Variations

- Usually involve right branch.
- **Absence of right branch (10-15%):** Portal vein trifurcates into left portal, right anterior, right posterior sectoral veins. Relative contraindication for split/live donor transplant.
- Right anterior sectoral vein can arise from hepatic portal vein.
- Right posterior sectoral vein can originate from left branch.
- Important to remember during left-sided liver resection.

## Porto-Systemic Shunts

- Increased pressure in portal venous system results in dilation of tributaries.
- Reversed flow at sites of porto-systemic anastomoses.
- Common sites listed in Table 69.1.

## Table 69.1: Porto-Systemic Anastomoses (Part 1)

| Portal Vein Tributary | Systemic Vein | Clinical Presentation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Left gastric vein | Distal oesophageal veins (draining to azygos/hemi-azygos) | Oesophageal and gastric varices |
| Superior anorectal veins | Middle and inferior anorectal veins (draining to internal iliac/pudendal) | Rectal varices |

## Table 69.1: Porto-Systemic Anastomoses (Part 2)

| Portal Vein Tributary | Systemic Vein | Clinical Presentation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Persistent tributaries in round ligament | Periumbilical branches of epigastric/intercostal veins | 'Caput medusae' |
| Tributaries overlying bare area | Retroperitoneal veins (azygos, lumbar, etc.) | Dilated retroperitoneal veins (risk during surgery) |
| Omental/colic veins near colic flexures | Retroperitoneal veins near flexures | Problematic during surgery |

## Hepatic Veins

- Liver drains by three major hepatic veins into suprahepatic IVC.
- Also via numerous minor hepatic veins into retrohepatic IVC.
- Adult retrohepatic IVC is 6-7 cm long, surrounded by segment I.
- Three major veins located between four sectors.
- Right hepatic vein: between right anterior and posterior sectors.
- Middle hepatic vein: between right and left hemilivers.
- Left hepatic vein: between left medial and lateral sectors.

## Right Hepatic Vein

- Longest and largest hepatic vein.
- Usually single, occasionally two trunks until termination.
- Runs in right portal fissure (between right medial and lateral sectors).
- Drains whole of segments VI and VII.
- Drains variable proportions of V and VIII.
- Formed anteriorly near inferior border.
- Drains into IVC near superior border of caudate lobe.
- Most variable in calibre.

## Middle Hepatic Vein

- Lies in main portal fissure (between right and left hemilivers).
- Usually joins left hepatic vein, terminates in IVC as short common trunk.
- Ends as single trunk in IVC in <10% of individuals.
- Drains central part of liver.
- Constant tributaries from segments IV, V, VIII.
- Vein from segment IV enters left side; vein from VIII enters right side.
- Intrahepatic anastomoses with right hepatic vein in up to one-third of adults.

## Left Hepatic Vein

- Lies between left medial and left lateral sectors.
- Drains segments II, III, and occasionally IV.
- Small veins from segment II and superior IV can drain directly into IVC.
- Umbilical fissure vein: major tributary running between segments III and IV.
- Occasionally, vein draining segment III ends separately in confluence of left and middle hepatic veins.
- Variations significant in split and live donor liver transplantation.

## Minor Hepatic Veins

- Segment I veins (1 to 5) drain directly into IVC.
- Venous drainage independent of rest of liver.
- Segment I often undergoes compensatory hypertrophy in Budd–Chiari syndrome.
- Accessory inferior or middle right hepatic veins can exist.
- Surgically important if >5 mm diameter.
- Drain segments V and VI independently.
- Must be individually anastomosed to recipient IVC in transplantation.

## TIPS Procedure

- **Transjugular intrahepatic Porto-Systemic Shunt.**
- For extreme chronic portal hypertension.
- Creates large calibre anastomosis between portal and systemic circulations within liver parenchyma.
- Stent inserted between large hepatic portal vein and hepatic vein.
- Introduced via internal jugular vein, guided radiologically.
- Relieves severe portal hypertension but tends to worsen hepatic encephalopathy.

## Lymphatic Drainage

- Lymph is rich in protein, product of hepatic sinusoids.
- Passes via deep and superficial pathways to nodes superior and inferior to diaphragm.
- Obstruction of hepatic venous drainage increases lymph flow in thoracic duct.

## Superficial Hepatic Lymphatics

- Run in subserosal loose connective tissue over liver surface.
- Drain in four directions:
  1. Most of posterior surface (including caudate lobe) → nodes alongside IVC.
  2. Posterior surface of left lobe → nodes around cardia of stomach.
  3. Coronary and right triangular ligaments → directly to thoracic duct.
  4. Most of inferior, anterior, superior surfaces → hepatic nodes at porta hepatis.
- Few from right superior surface → coeliac nodes.

## Deep Hepatic Lymphatics

- Fine lymphatics within portal triads and around interlobular veins.
- Merge to form larger vessels.
- Some ascend through parenchyma to caval foramen → inferior mediastinum nodes.
- Most drain to lymph nodes at porta hepatis.
- Travel within lesser omentum to drain to lateral aortic nodes.

## Innervation

- Parenchyma supplied by nerves from hepatic plexus entering at porta hepatis.
- Some nerve fibres arise from right phrenic nerve (basis of referred shoulder pain in biliary colic).
- Fibrous capsule supplied by fine branches of inferior intercostal nerves.
- Supply parietal peritoneum around bare area and superior surface.
- Distension/disruption of fibrous capsule causes well-localised sharp pain.

## Hepatic Plexus

- Receives preganglionic parasympathetic fibres from anterior (and posterior) vagal trunk.
- Receives postganglionic sympathetic fibres via coeliac and superior mesenteric plexuses.
- Nerve fibres accompany portal triad branches into liver, penetrating to hepatocytes.
- Aminergic, cholinergic, peptidergic, nitrergic fibres identified.
- Involved in hepatic metabolism and control of sinusoidal blood flow.
- Transplanted (denervated) liver shows this role is not essential.

## Referred Pain

- Pain from liver parenchyma is poorly localised.
- Referred to epigastric region (foregut origin).
- Stretch/irritation of fibrous capsule by inflammation/neoplasia produces well-localised 'somatic' pain.
- Pathology involving diaphragmatic surface referred via phrenic nerve to right shoulder region (C3–5 dermatomes).

## Microstructure Overview

- Epithelial–mesenchymal outgrowth of caudal foregut.
- Connected via biliary tree.
- Surface covered by serosa (visceral peritoneum).
- Beneath this: thin (50–100 μm) capsule of connective tissue.
- Extensions pass into liver as septa and trabeculae.
- Portal tracts contain hepatic artery, portal vein, bile ductules/ducts.
- **Portal triad:** combination of two blood vessels and a bile duct, plus lymphatics and nerves.

## Figure 69.16: Structural Organization

![Figure 69.16: The structural organisation of the liver. A, Lobules. B, A portal triad. C, Functional view showing acini and zones.](figure_69_16.png)

## Liver Parenchyma

- Complex network of epithelial cells (hepatocytes).
- Supported by connective tissue.
- Perfused by rich blood supply from portal vein and hepatic artery.
- Hepatocytes carry out major metabolic activities.
- Other cells have storage, phagocytic, and supportive functions.
- Hepatocytes arranged in plates (one cell thick), separated by venous sinusoids.

## Bile Secretion and Fetal Liver

- Bile secreted by hepatocytes.
- Collected in network of minute channels (canaliculi) between hepatocyte membranes.
- Hepatocytes act as exocrine cells.
- Fetal liver is a major haemopoietic organ.
- Erythrocytes, leukocytes, platelets develop from mesenchyme covering sinusoidal endothelium.

## Figure 69.17: Sinusoidal Organization

![Figure 69.17: Scanning electron micrographs of resin corrosion cast demonstrating 3D arrangement of hepatic sinusoids.](figure_69_17.png)

## Lobulation of the Liver

- Structural unit is the lobule: roughly hexagonal arrangement of plates.
- Separated by sinusoids radiating from central vein.
- Portal triads at vertices of hexagon.
- Central veins drain into hepatic veins.
- Human lobules lack distinct boundaries/connective tissue septa.
- Plates run irregularly, anastomosing and branching.

## Liver Acini

- Functional unit revealed by 3D reconstruction.
- Ovoid mass of tissue orientated around terminal branches of hepatic arteriole and portal venule.
- Long axis defined by two adjacent central veins.
- **Acinar functional heterogeneity:** related to blood supply.
  - **Zone 1:** Periportal zone.
  - **Zone 2:** Intermediate zone.
  - **Zone 3:** Perivenous (pericentral/centrilobular) zone.
- Clarified interpretation of histopathology (hypoxic damage, toxic injury).

## Blood Supply in Microstructure

- Preterminal hepatic arterioles convey arterial blood to sinusoids.
- Mostly via fine capillary plexus draining to portal vein branches.
- Small proportion passes directly to sinusoids.
- Sinusoids contain mixed venous and arterial blood.
- Central veins form interlobular veins → hepatic veins → IVC.

## Hepatic Plates and Sinusoids

- Endothelium of sinusoids is fenestrated.
- Lacks continuous basal lamina (acts as dynamic blood filter).
- Perisinusoidal space (of Disse) separates sinusoids from hepatocyte plates.
- 0.2–0.5 μm wide (distends in hypoxic states).
- Contains interstitial fluid, hepatocyte microvilli, stellate cells, collagen fibres, nerve terminals.

## Bile Canaliculi

- Network of minute interconnecting channels (~1 μm diameter).
- Run between hepatic plates.
- Formed by apposed plasma membranes of adjacent hepatocytes.
- Sealed by tight junctions isolating lumen from intercellular space.
- Conduct bile to bile canals (of Hering) lined by cholangiocytes and hepatocytes.
- Canals empty into bile ductules → interlobular bile ducts.
- Bile flow is towards periphery (opposite to centripetal blood flow).

## Cells of the Liver

- Hepatocytes
- Hepatic stellate cells (perisinusoidal, fat-storing, Ito cells)
- Sinusoidal endothelial cells
- Stellate macrophages (Kupffer cells)
- Cholangiocytes
- Hepatic stem cells
- Hepatic natural killer lymphocytes (pit cells)
- Connective tissue cells of capsule and portal tracts

## Hepatocytes: Structure

- 80% of liver volume, 60% of cellular population.
- Polyhedral (5–12 sides), 20–30 μm across.
- Nuclei round, euchromatic, often tetraploid/polyploid/multiple.
- Cytoplasm contains rough/smooth ER, mitochondria, lysosomes, Golgi apparatus.
- Glycogen granules, lipid vacuoles, peroxisomes, enzyme vacuoles prominent.
- Storage vacuoles containing ferritin and haemosiderin (iron metabolism).

## Hepatocytes: Surface Features

- Sinusoidal surface exhibits microvilli (~0.5 μm long).
- Creates large surface area (~70% of hepatocyte surface) exposed to blood plasma.
- Linked by gap junctions and desmosomes.
- Lateral plasma membranes form bile canaliculi.
- Sealed by tight junctions (occludins, claudins, junctional adhesion molecules, CAR).
- Prevent bile from entering interstitial fluid (blood–bile barrier).

## Hepatic Stellate Cells

- Much less numerous than hepatocytes.
- Lie within perisinusoidal space (of Disse).
- Irregular outline.
- Characterised by cytoplasmic lipid droplets storing fat-soluble vitamin A.
- Secrete intralobular matrix components (collagen type III/reticular fibres).
- Significant source of growth factors in homeostasis/regeneration.
- **Role in pathology:** Become myofibroblast-like in liver injury. Replace damaged hepatocytes with collagenous scar tissue (fibrosis). Starts in zone 3. Can progress to cirrhosis.

## Sinusoidal Endothelial Cells

- Sinusoids wider than capillaries.
- Lined by thin, highly fenestrated endothelium.
- Lacks complete basal lamina.
- Cells flattened, central nucleus, joined by junctional complexes.
- Fenestrae grouped in clusters (~100 nm mean diameter).
- Allows plasma direct access to hepatocyte basal membranes.
- Cytoplasm contains numerous transcytotic vesicles.

## Stellate Macrophages (Kupffer Cells)

- Derived from circulating blood monocytes (bone marrow origin).
- Long-term hepatic residents.
- Lie within sinusoidal lumina attached to endothelial surface.
- More concentrated in periportal zones.
- Largest population of mononuclear phagocyte system.
- Remove cellular/microbial debris, secrete cytokines.
- Implicated in endotoxin tolerance, transplantation, NAFLD, alcoholic liver disease.
- Remove aged/damaged RBCs (shared with spleen, fulfilled entirely by liver after splenectomy).

## Hepatic Stem Cells

- Undifferentiated pluripotent cells.
- Reside around bile canals.
- Derived from ductal plate in fetal livers.
- Progeny are small epithelial cells (8–18 μm).
- Large oval nuclei, scanty cytoplasm.
- Express both biliary epithelial and hepatocyte markers.

## Figure 69.18: Hepatic Microstructure

![Figure 69.18: Hepatic microstructure: sinusoidal endothelial cells are not shown.](figure_69_18.png)

## Summary

- The liver is a complex organ with critical metabolic, immune, and digestive functions.
- Its anatomy is highly segmented, which dictates surgical approaches.
- Dual blood supply (hepatic artery and portal vein) and unique venous drainage.
- Microstructurally organized into functional acini with distinct metabolic zones.
- Composed of diverse cell populations ensuring homeostasis and regeneration.
